text:
No single combo is best for every RV. The right one depends on how much power you use. The sources I could read were thin on prices and exact panel pairings, so check current prices before you buy.

## My picks

**1. Best all-rounder for a typical RV: ALLPOWERS R4000 with 400–800 W of solar**
- It has 3,456 Wh of LiFePO4 battery (3,500+ cycles) and 3,600 W continuous AC output, with 6,000 W peak. It also has a dedicated RV outlet and a 5-year warranty.
- It accepts up to 2,000 W of solar across three inputs, each taking up to 650 W (12–60 V).
- Its AC input is 2,000 W, so it recharges from shore power in about 2 hours.
- It currently costs $1,319.12 with code EXTRA12. The list price is $1,499, and the code needs an order over $1,200. It expires 2026-11-15, and the page says it was checked in the cart on 2026-10-23.
- Solar panels are not included, so you'd buy them separately.
- [Buy the ALLPOWERS R4000](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh). This is an affiliate link, so the site earns a commission if you buy through it. I could only confirm the specs from that site's own page, so check the manufacturer's checkout before you pay.

**2. Best for heavy loads and future expansion: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- It has 4,096 Wh, expandable past 12 kWh, with 4,000 W running and 8,000 W surge output.
- It's quiet (under 30 dBA at low load) and charges from 0 to 80% on AC in about 50 minutes.
- It's heavy enough to need two people to move. Its solar input and price weren't stated in the source.

**3. Best for a built-in 30A RV outlet at lower capacity: BLUETTI AC200L**
- It has 2,048 Wh and 2,400 W running (3,600 W surge), and it connects straight to a folding solar array.
- It has no 240V output, and it runs at about 50 dBA at full load.

**Others to consider**
- **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro:** 3,024 Wh and up to about 1,400 W of solar charging. It has no 30A RV outlet, so you need an adapter.
- **Anker SOLIX F2600:** 2,560 Wh with a 30A outlet, but lower solar input than the flagships.
- **Goal Zero Yeti 1,500X:** 1,516 Wh and the lightest of the group at about 44 lb. It needs a soft-start kit to run a 13,500 BTU roof AC.

## Sizing and pairing tips
- **Roof AC:** An air conditioner drawing about 1,500 W drains these units in about 2 hours. Plan on shore power or a generator for AC. Use the battery for the fridge, lights, devices and fans.
- **Solar size:** The EmergencyEnergy guide suggests 300–400 W of folding panels for mid-size units. A 300 W panel refills a 1,500 Wh unit in about 6 hours of good summer sun. For a 3,000+ Wh unit, I'd aim for 600 W or more of solar, which also fits the ALLPOWERS R4000's inputs.
- **Panel specs:** Check that the panel voltage (12–60 V on the R4000) and connectors match your station. Use adapters if they don't.
- **Roof panels or folding panels:** Folding panels can sit in the shade or follow the sun. Roof panels are more convenient but fixed in place.

## Sources
- [EmergencyEnergy: RV Power Station Comparison](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/). It had no prices, and some of its text is Ontario-focused.
- [Acquired Sense: Best Portable Power Stations 2026](https://www.acquiredsense.com/reviews/power-stations.html). It had only brand-level info, and its buy links looked like placeholders, so I left them out.
- [Dealectric: ALLPOWERS R4000](https://dealectric.com/lab/V3/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)

If you tell me your RV type, your biggest loads (AC, microwave, fridge, CPAP) and your budget, I can narrow this to one station and a specific panel setup.
